findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The cache check uses check-then-act across two separate lock acquisitions (RLock to read, then release, then acquire the write Lock), so two concurrent cold-start requests both observe nil and both perform the full asset scan serially under the write lock. Non-Dev users hitting a cold cache concurrently (e.g., right after process start) each pay the full directory scan instead of one doing the work and the rest reusing the result; the second writer also overwrites the first result, which is benign today but makes the 'cached' invariant weaker than it appears for future maintainers.

[ADVISORY] The double-checked locking pattern never re-checks entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent cache misses on a cold cache all serialize on the mutex and each rebuild the asset scan instead of one builder publishing for the rest. Operators of multi-Grafana-instance or high-concurrency startups see N serialized full asset builds at first request; correctness is preserved but the lock is held across the entire expensive build, delaying even the fast Dev path's cache reads behind a queue of writers.

[BUG] The new mutex-guarded cache logic is concurrency-relevant non-trivial logic introduced by this diff with no accompanying test (no test-shaped file appears anywhere in the diff), leaving the lock ordering and Dev-mode read path unverified. A regression in the lock discipline (e.g., a future caller invoking GetWebAssets while holding another lock, or a missed unlock in an added early-return) produces a deadlock or data race in production that the test suite cannot catch; the code path returns a shared *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer to all request goroutines, and any caller-side mutation of that shared cached struct races with no test exercising concurrent access.

[ADVISORY] The double-checked locking pattern is incomplete: after acquiring the write lock there is no re-check of entryPointAssetsCache, so the second-through-Nth concurrent requester each rebuild the assets while holding the exclusive lock. Under a cold-start burst (N simultaneous first requests in non-Dev), the file scan/build runs N times serialized behind the mutex, adding latency exactly on the high-concurrency path the PR claims to optimize; the fix is a one-line nil re-check inside the critical section.

[BUG] The cache check is not repeated after acquiring the write lock, so this is broken double-checked locking: every concurrent first-request goroutine rebuilds the assets and overwrites the cache. N simultaneous requests on a cold cache each perform the full filesystem scan/rebuild serially under the write lock, and each reassigns entryPointAssetsCache, discarding the result the previous goroutine just computed — wasted work proportional to concurrent load and lock hold time, with no fast-path recheck after blocking.

[BUG] The cached *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer is returned to callers without a defensive copy, so any caller that mutates the returned struct corrupts the shared cache for all subsequent requests. A middleware or handler that appends to or edits fields on the returned EntryPointAssets (a natural thing to do per-request, e.g. adding a plugin entry point) permanently mutates the process-wide cached value, causing data races on subsequent reads under only RLock (which guards the pointer swap, not the pointed-to struct) and cross-tenant/cross-request leakage of one caller's mutations into every other response.

[BUG] In Dev mode the function takes the exclusive write lock and holds it (defer Unlock) across the full asset-scan / manifest-reading work that follows, so all concurrent requests serialize behind one mutex doing disk I/O. Every Dev-mode request that misses the cache blocks on entryPointAssetsCacheMu while one goroutine performs filesystem scans; a fresh `grafana server` startup with N concurrent browser/asset requests turns into a serial queue of full scans (Dev never populates the cache per the original guard, so this re-serializes on every request), causing visible multi-second stalls in local development and a potential request pileup behind the lock.

[ADVISORY] The cache is read-checked before acquiring the write lock but never re-checked under it, so the mutex does not actually deduplicate concurrent rebuilds — it merely serializes them. On a cold start under concurrent load (e.g. multiple requests arriving before the first build finishes), every request performs the full asset-scan/build work in turn, defeating the point of the lock; whoever deploys this expecting single-flight gets N serialized rebuilds instead. Correctness is preserved (all callers eventually get a valid result), so this is a latency/waste concern, not data corruption.

goldens.comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

adjudication.rationale: The diff implements an RWMutex-protected cache with an initial read-lock fast path, but after falling through it acquires the write lock (`entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`) without re-checking whether another goroutine populated `entryPointAssetsCache` while it was blocked. On a cold cache with concurrent callers, each goroutine that saw `nil` will later run the rebuild path serially under the write lock and reassign the cache, causing wasted work/latency. This is verifiable from the shown code, but it’s primarily a performance/concurrency efficiency issue rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `GetWebAssets` returns the global cached pointer (`ret := entryPointAssetsCache` then `return ret, nil`) and the new `RWMutex` only guards access to the cache pointer itself, not the contents of the `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` it points to. If callers mutate the returned struct, they would be mutating shared global state. However, the diff does not show any caller mutations or that `EntryPointAssets` is treated as mutable per-request, so the claimed corruption/race is plausible but not directly verifiable from this diff alone.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly adds an RWMutex and, on a cache miss (or always in Dev), takes entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() with a deferred Unlock() that will cover the remaining work in GetWebAssets. That means any expensive asset scanning/manifest reading done later in the function will run under the exclusive lock, serializing concurrent calls. This is a real, diff-grounded performance/scalability concern, especially in Dev where the early-return cache path is disabled (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil { return ret }`), but it’s not a correctness defect that can be proven broken from the shown lines.

adjudication.rationale: In GetWebAssets, the code does an RLock/RUnlock to read entryPointAssetsCache into ret and only returns early if ret != nil. If ret is nil, it then takes the write lock (Lock) but does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache under that write lock before proceeding to rebuild. This means concurrent callers on a cold cache will each miss the initial check and then run the rebuild work one-by-one under the mutex (serialized rebuilds rather than single-flight deduplication). This is a real, diff-grounded performance/latency concern, not a correctness defect.
